clips.title: AWS EC2 Instance types Explained | AWS SAA C03
clips.why: How to read an instance type's name, followed by the general purpose family that m8i belongs to.
look: The parts of the name: family, generation, extra letters, then the size after the dot.
What "general purpose" means: a balance of processors and memory, the right fit for builds and tests.
clips.after: lite, full and wide are the same m8i family in three sizes, so one image fits all of them.

clips.title: Simplify and speed up your EC2 instance creation process with EC2 Launch Templates
clips.why: A short walk through creating a launch template in the console, so you can see the questions it saves the answers to.
look: Every field in the form is one answer that no launch has to repeat.
The AMI is chosen inside the template; ours points at an SSM parameter instead of a fixed image.
clips.after: Our templates are written in code instead of the console, but they save the same answers: image, size, role, disk and metadata rules.

clips.title: Transition to IMDSv2 on EC2 - Introduction, Preparation, Pitfalls
clips.why: A careful comparison of IMDSv1 and IMDSv2 by an experienced AWS consultant: what the token adds and which attacks it stops.
look: The plain GET of IMDSv1 against the PUT-then-GET of IMDSv2, the same two requests you send in the lab.
Why a server that fetches URLs for a user was enough to steal credentials with IMDSv1.
The hop limit, and why it matters for containers.
clips.after: Our launch templates require IMDSv2 with hop limit 1, so neither a tricked URL fetcher nor a container on the VM can read the role's credentials.

practice.q: Complete the metadata option that turns IMDSv1 off.
practice.hint: The other value, optional, keeps the old plain GET working.
practice.why: With required, every request needs a token from a PUT, and a plain GET gets 401.

practice.q: A full VM is m8i.2xlarge. What is a wide VM, with twice the processors and memory?

options.why: Sizes double at each step, and the step after 2xlarge is 4xlarge.
That number is the generation, not the size. A newer generation is not a bigger machine.
Same family and generation, next size: 16 processors and 64 GiB instead of 8 and 32.

practice.q: Put the IMDSv2 flow of a program on the VM in order.
items: The program sends a PUT to /latest/api/token with a time-to-live header
IMDS answers with a token, in a reply that can travel only one hop
The program sends a GET for iam/security-credentials/ with the token in a header
IMDS answers with the role's temporary credentials
The program signs its AWS requests with them until they expire
practice.why: The PUT with its header is what a tricked URL fetcher cannot do, and the one-hop reply is what a container cannot receive.

practice.q: The nightly build made a new image, and it passed its smoke test. What changes so that new VMs boot from it?

options.text: Every launch template gets a new version with the new AMI ID
options.why: That would work, but it is what the parameter avoids. The templates never change for a new image.

options.text: The SSM parameter /ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id gets the new image ID
options.why: The templates say resolve:ssm:/ai-agents/sandbox/ami-id, so one write promotes the image for all three sizes.

options.text: Each running VM is updated in place to the new image
options.why: VMs are never updated in place. New ones boot from the new image, and old ones are replaced.

practice.q: Which of these does the sandbox launch template deliberately leave out?

options.text: An SSH key and a public address
options.why: Nobody logs in to a sandbox and nothing from the internet should reach it. Commands arrive through Systems Manager instead.
The template names the instance profile. The role exists, it is just near-empty.
The tags are essential: the sweeper finds sandbox VMs and disks by ai-agents:managed=true.
